title: Network Defense
description: Tools and techniques to protect networks: defense in depth, segmentation, firewalls, IDS/IPS inspection and detection methods, and endpoint security.

nodes.title: Defense in Depth
nodes.description:
Multiple layers of controls, so that if one control fails, the crown jewels (the valuable assets) are not exposed.
At each layer of defense, use at least a combination of preventive, detective and corrective controls.
Example of adding layers:
- Instead of a single firewall between the internet and all systems, including internet-facing web, mail and FTP servers, segment the network and move those servers into a DMZ.
- Add a second firewall to create a screened subnet architecture, perhaps from a different firewall vendor.
- Beyond preventive controls, add an IDS for detection, or an IPS for detection and correction.
All this technology must be balanced against the value of the assets being protected. Controls must be cost effective.

nodes.title: Network Segmentation / Partitioning
nodes.description:
Break a network into pieces, then control the flow of traffic between them and apply different levels of control to each piece.
Example: a guest network that is only allowed out to the internet, with very limited controls, and a part of the network holding back-end, high-value databases, with extensive controls to prevent and detect unauthorized access.

children.title: Network Perimeter
children.description:
The largest segmentation: between the organization's internal network and the internet.
Ideally, the internal network and the public-facing side are clearly separated, and the flow of traffic between them is controlled, typically with a firewall.
Never use the idea of an internal trusted network. Always assume attackers are inside your network. There is no trusted network: Zero Trust.

children.title: DMZ
children.description:
A network segment for bastion hosts, the systems that are intentionally reachable by the public over the internet, such as web, mail and FTP servers.
These systems are expected to be attacked. If one is compromised inside this segment, the attacker does not have a foothold in the internal network.
Traffic from this segment into the internal network is severely restricted. It is essentially connected only out to the internet.

children.title: Bastion Host
children.description:
Computers or servers specifically configured to withstand attacks.
Typically a public-facing server, such as a web server, placed in a DMZ.

children.title: Proxy
children.description:
A server located between two devices. It acts as an intermediary: all traffic between the devices must pass through it.
This lets the proxy read, filter and control the communications, and even hide the devices behind it.

children.title: NAT / PAT
children.description:
Examples of proxies.
- NAT: remaps (swaps) one IP address for another by modifying the IP header of packets as they pass through the proxy. Typically an internal, unroutable IP address is remapped to a publicly routable address as a packet goes out to the internet. For returning responses, the proxy changes the destination address from its own IP address back to the internal system's IP address.
- PAT: the same idea, but many internal systems share one public IP address, and the proxy tells their connections apart by remapping port numbers.
Full names: Network Address Translation; Port Address Translation.

nodes.title: Firewalls
nodes.description:
One of the most fundamental tools in network security.
At the most basic level, these devices control the flow of traffic between network segments. Example: what traffic from the internet is allowed through to the internal network.

children.title: Types
children.description:
Firewalls have evolved a lot over the years and become much smarter about how they inspect traffic and decide what to allow through.
Be able to compare the core types, so you can choose the right one for a network segment or security requirement.
Most modern firewalls offer the capabilities of all these types: quick, simple decisions from the packet header, and much deeper analysis of packet contents when needed. You get speed and intelligence where you want them.

children.title: Packet Filtering
children.description:
The oldest and simplest type. Inspects only packet headers: source and destination IP addresses and ports, checked against a set of rules, typically an Access Control List (ACL).
Not very smart, but extremely efficient: very fast decisions and very low latency, so traffic is barely slowed down.
Operates at layer 3, the network layer.

children.title: Stateful Packet Filtering
children.description:
Still looks only at packet headers, but keeps a table of connections: a little memory with a history of recent traffic through the firewall.
Example: two systems complete the TCP three-way handshake (SYN, SYN/ACK, ACK). The firewall records that they have an established connection and will likely allow their packets. A TCP packet from another system out of the blue is likely blocked, because there is no record of it setting up a connection.
In short: if it sees a packet go out, it allows the reply back in, because it remembers the outgoing packet.
Operates at layer 3, the network layer.

children.title: Circuit Proxy
children.description:
Operates at layer 5, the session layer.
Understands what is happening at the session layer, and allows a session to be set up if it complies with predefined rules.

children.title: Application
children.description:
Application firewalls operate at layer 7, the application layer.
They do deep packet inspection: they can inspect anything in the packet header, and reassemble a series of packets to inspect the data being sent. Example: scan a file being sent for viruses.
Very intelligent, able to make very sophisticated decisions. But this costs speed: they are the slowest type of firewall, with the highest latency.

nodes.title: Inspection
nodes.description: The major network monitoring tools, IDS and IPS systems, and other ways to detect suspicious activity on a network.

children.title: IDS
children.description:
Inspects network traffic (packets) to detect potentially suspicious activity. If it detects something suspicious, it raises an alarm, but does not block anything on its own.
It can work with, for example, a firewall to block traffic.
Full name: Intrusion Detection System.

children.title: IPS
children.description:
Does exactly what an IDS does, then goes a step further. If it detects something suspicious, it can block the traffic, preventing an attack.
It can detect and block traffic on its own.
Full name: Intrusion Prevention System.

children.title: IDS/IPS Location
children.description: The two major places to put an IDS or IPS.

children.title: Host Based
children.description:
Installed on a specific host, typically a high-value server, and monitors only that host.
To monitor several hosts, each one needs its own IDS or IPS installed.

children.title: Network Based
children.description:
Connected to a network segment, and monitors all the traffic in that segment.
There are two ways to connect it to the segment.

children.title: In-line
children.description:
All traffic coming in and out of the network segment must pass through the IDS or IPS.
IPSs are often installed in-line. The advantage: all traffic passes through the IPS, so it can easily block traffic it does not like.
The major downside: it is another point of failure. If the device goes down or fails secure, all traffic is blocked, causing a denial of service.

children.title: Mirror, Span, Promiscuous
children.description:
The IDS or IPS is connected to a switch port that is configured as a mirror, span or promiscuous port.
By default, a switch forwards packets only to the intended system, so the IDS or IPS would not see most of the traffic. With a mirror port, all packets going through the switch are copied to the IDS or IPS, so it can monitor everything.
IDSs are more commonly installed this way.

children.title: IDS / IPS Detection Methods
children.description: The two major ways an IDS or IPS looks for suspicious activity are pattern matching and anomaly detection. It can also use allow and deny lists, and sandboxes.

children.title: Pattern
children.description:
Pattern matching: the IDS or IPS is programmed to look for a specific pattern, such as a specific type of network attack, and alerts or blocks when it detects it.
Fast and efficient, but it can only detect what it has been programmed to detect.

children.title: Signature analysis
children.description:
How a pattern-matching IDS or IPS is told which patterns to look for.
Each known type of network attack has a unique fingerprint, such as byte sequences in network traffic or known malicious instruction sequences. The IDS or IPS compares traffic against a database of these fingerprints.

children.title: Anomaly
children.description:
Does not rely on signatures. It addresses the weakness of pattern matching, which can only detect what it has been programmed to detect.
The IDS or IPS learns what normal looks like (it establishes a baseline), then looks for behavior that falls outside the accepted model.
There are four major ways to spot such deviations.

children.title: Stateful matching
children.description:
Looks at a whole conversation between systems, not single packets.
The IDS or IPS keeps a table of open sessions, so it can detect, for example, a system sending TCP packets to another system it has not set up a session with.

children.title: Statistical
children.description: Compares traffic to typical, known or predicted traffic profiles, looking for statistically significant deviations from the norm.

children.title: Protocol
children.description:
Detects anomalies based on the network protocols in use. Certain protocols are defined as allowed, and any other protocol is an anomaly.
Example: an organization allows only SFTP. FTP traffic, or especially TFTP traffic, is an anomaly.

children.title: Traffic
children.description: Identifies anomalies in the expected pattern and behavior of network traffic sent within a session, such as an unusual volume or an unusual time of day.

children.title: White & Black Lists
children.description:
An IDS or IPS can inspect traffic against approved or banned addresses:
- Allow list: the IPs a system is allowed to connect to. All other IPs are blocked.
- Deny list: the IPs a system is not allowed to connect to. All other IPs are allowed.
'Allow list' and 'deny list' are the better, modern names.

children.title: Sandbox
children.description:
A safe area to run untrusted code and watch what it does, for example trying to install ransomware.
An IDS or IPS can detect that an executable is being transmitted, run a copy of it in a sandbox, and, if it does something nefarious, alert and possibly block the file from reaching the intended victim.

children.title: Honeypots & honeynets
children.description:
A decoy system that looks as close as possible to a real system, such as a file server, print server, database or industrial control system. But it is not a real system used by employees or clients.
It is carefully monitored. Anyone trying to connect to and use it is a very good sign that a threat actor is in the network, exploring for systems to compromise.
One decoy is a single system; a whole network of decoys can also be built.
A good way to detect Advanced Persistent Threats.

children.title: Ingress vs. Egress
children.description:
Monitoring the traffic coming into a network, for example from the internet, and the traffic leaving it.
Organizations often detect a breach by watching outbound traffic. Traffic going out to a known bad IP address is a good sign that malware has infected a company system and is calling home.

nodes.title: Endpoint Security
nodes.description:
A network can never be secure if the devices connected to it are not secure: laptops, mobile phones, iPads, Alexa devices, IP security cameras and so on.
Harden these devices: make sure they are correctly configured, patched, use strong authentication and so forth.
Covered in the Vulnerabilities in Systems mind map (Domain 3).
